meta.title: Predicting Heart Failure Outcomes with Machine Learning
meta.subtitle: An MSc Research Journal
meta.tagline: Can a machine learning model predict which heart failure patients are most at risk — before they leave the hospital?
meta.research_question: Can machine learning models, trained on clinical data available at the point of hospital discharge, accurately predict multi-horizon adverse outcomes in heart failure patients — and can those predictions be made clinically interpretable through explainability methods?

about.heading: What This Project Is
about.text: This project builds a machine learning tool that predicts which heart failure patients are most at risk of dying or returning to hospital after discharge. It uses a publicly available, anonymised dataset of 2,008 real patients and 166 clinical variables — one of only five such datasets available worldwide.

about.heading: Why This Matters
about.text: One in three heart failure patients is readmitted within six months of discharge. Often this happens because nobody flagged them as high risk when they left the ward. This tool does that flagging — and explains its reasoning in plain clinical language so a cardiologist can trust it.

about.heading: What Success Looks Like
about.text: The existing benchmark (Chicco & Jurman, 2020) achieved an AUROC of 0.73 using just 2 clinical variables. This project uses all 166 variables with gradient-boosted models and targets AUROC ≥ 0.80, with SHAP explanations validated by clinical experts.

about.heading: Four Things We Predict
about.text: Death within 28 days. Death within 3 months. Death within 6 months. Readmission within 6 months. Predicting across all four timepoints gives a complete risk picture — not just a single number — for every patient.

journal.entry:
The first week was entirely reading — no code, no data. It felt slow at first but it was absolutely necessary. I didn't realise how much clinical context matters until I looked at a variable called 'tricuspid valve return velocity' and had no idea what it measured or why it matters. Now I understand that it's used to estimate pulmonary artery pressure — a key marker of right heart strain in heart failure.

The most surprising thing I learned: 30-day readmission is considered more important than 30-day mortality in cardiology. Hospitals are judged on it. Preventing a patient from coming back to hospital within a month is arguably harder than keeping them alive in the initial admission — and my dataset captures both.

The literature gap became very clear: every paper I read either predicted a single outcome, used a dataset of under 1,000 patients, or didn't explain the model's reasoning. Mine does all three differently.

key_papers.finding: Describes our exact dataset. 2,008 patients, 166 variables, Chinese hospital. Authors note the dataset's richness but provide no predictive modelling — that's our work.
Showed that just 2 variables (creatinine and LVEF) can predict heart failure survival with reasonable accuracy. Benchmark AUC: 0.73.
key_papers.relevance: Baseline to beat — we use 166 variables

key_papers.citation: Lundberg et al. (2020) — Nature Machine Intelligence
key_papers.finding: Introduced SHAP values for explaining tree-based models. Now standard in clinical ML for making predictions interpretable to clinicians.

tasks.summary: Mapped missingness across all 166 variables. Found cholinesterase 100% missing (dropped). LVEF missing in 68% — requires careful imputation strategy. 121 variables have under 30% missing data.

tasks.summary: Defined 4 prediction targets. 6-month mortality: 2.8% positive rate (severe imbalance). 6-month readmission: 38.5% (more balanced). Will use SMOTE and class weighting strategies.

glossary.definition: A hormone released by the heart muscle when it is under stress or stretched. High levels indicate the heart is struggling to pump effectively. A standard clinical marker for heart failure severity.
glossary.clinical_note: Dataset range: 2.7–5,000 pg/mL. Clinical danger threshold: >400 pg/mL. Mean in this dataset: ~1,280 pg/mL — the average patient is already in danger territory.

glossary.definition: The percentage of blood pumped out of the left ventricle with each heartbeat. A healthy heart ejects 55–70%. Below 40% is classified as reduced ejection fraction — the heart is too weak.
glossary.clinical_note: Measured by echocardiogram. Missing in 68% of this dataset because not every patient received a scan. Handling this missing data correctly is a key methodological challenge.

glossary.definition: A four-level scale (I–IV) describing how severely heart failure limits a patient's daily activities. Class I: no limitation. Class IV: symptoms even at rest — the most severe.
glossary.clinical_note: In this dataset: 52% Class III, 31% Class IV. This is an exceptionally sick cohort, which explains the serious outcomes.

glossary.abbr: Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve
glossary.definition: A performance metric for classification models. Ranges from 0.5 (random guessing) to 1.0 (perfect prediction). Measures the model's ability to distinguish between patients who will and will not have a bad outcome.
glossary.clinical_note: Benchmark (Chicco & Jurman 2020): 0.73. This project targets ≥ 0.80 using 166 variables and gradient-boosted models.

glossary.definition: A method from game theory adapted for machine learning. For every prediction, SHAP calculates exactly how much each variable contributed — making black-box models explainable to clinicians.
glossary.clinical_note: Produces global summary plots (which variables matter overall) and patient-level waterfall charts (why this specific patient is high risk). Now standard in clinical ML.

glossary.definition: A statistical technique for handling missing data. Instead of filling gaps with a simple average, MICE uses all other available variables to intelligently estimate what a missing value most likely was.
glossary.clinical_note: Used here to handle up to 68% missingness in LVEF and other variables. Far superior to mean imputation, which would distort clinical distributions.
